https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg4.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Kevin Rideout was kidnapped outside his home in Niger's capital Niamey (file photo) By Chris Ewokor ,Â BBC Africa, Â and Â Amy Walker Published 14 August 2026 An American missionary has been released after spending more than nine months in captivity, the international Christian organisation he worked for has said. Kevin Rideout - who was kidnapped outside his home in Niger's capital Niamey last year - was "in good health in the care of US officials", SIM International said in a statement on Friday. The New York Times, which first reported Rideout's release, cited unnamed US officials saying that he was now in FBI custody, though details of how he was released, as well as who he had been held by, remained unclear. There had been concerns that Rideout had been taken by militants, who have increasingly used violence and abductions as tactics. Rideout's kidnapping in October was carried out by three armed men who took him to the western Tillaberi region, a location known as a hotbed of militant activity, news agency Reuters reported, citing diplomatic sources. It was feared he may have been taken there by militants belonging to groups like Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate which has been linked to several attacks in the region. Islamist militant groups operating from neighbouring Nigeria, Mali and Burkina Faso have plagued Niger for years, targeting both civilians and the military. The region has seen a wave of violence as jihadists have been fighting government security forces as well as Western and other allied troops. Within days of Rideout's kidnapping, the US warned its citizens against travelling to Niger due to an "increased risk of terrorism, crime and civil unrest". The New York Times reported that Rideout, who is also a pilot, may have been transferred to another group prior to his release. SIM International said he would soon be reunited with his wife, their children and his extended family. Rideout had been working in Niger as a Christian missionary for 19 years and was also a pilot for SIM International, which operates in more than 70 countries. The organisation said Rideout's release was "incredibly good news" after months of uncertainty about his wellbeing. "Krista and the rest of Kevin's family are profoundly grateful for the prayers offered on their behalf by people around the world throughout his captivity," it said. It added that the family had requested privacy while they "reconnect after this time apart". Rideout's release comes as several countries in West Africa and the Sahel have been struggling with terror attacks. Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and Nigeria have been dealing with violence that has been going on for more than a decade - resulting in the loss of thousands of lives and causing regional destabilisation. The region has also experienced a wave of military takeovers, with a string of democratic governments overthrown. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: After Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke at the UN, South Korea’s president Lee Jae Myung claimed Ukraine had broken a non-disclosure agreement between the two countries. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP View image in fullscreen After Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke at the UN, South Korea’s president Lee Jae Myung claimed Ukraine had broken a non-disclosure agreement between the two countries. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP South Korea Explainer Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war? Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s mention during a UN speech that Kyiv had sent two prisoners of war to South Korea has spiralled into a most unexpected crisis Raphael Rashid in Seoul Tue 29 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 04.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google South Korea and Ukraine are locked in an escalating diplomatic dispute over who agreed what regarding the circumstances of two prisoners of war captured fighting for Russia. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , told the UN general assembly last week that his country had “sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea”. Seoul had long said it would take the men. But rather than celebrate, on Monday South Korea summoned Ukraine’s most senior diplomat in Seoul and demanded an apology. Here’s a brief guide to what has happened, and why. Who are the PoWs and what has happened to them? Ukrainian forces captured the two men in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were among thousands of troops Pyongyang sent to fight for Moscow. Both men later said they wanted to go to South Korea, which regards North Koreans as its own citizens . Ukraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in Russia Read more In July, Zelenskyy and South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung , agreed to resolve the issue while respecting the soldiers’ “free will”. The captured pair reportedly arrived in South Korea via a third country earlier this month. North Koreans arriving in the South as defectors are usually questioned by the National Intelligence Service before being sent to a state resettlement centre, although sensitive cases can reportedly bypass the centre. Why is Seoul so angry? Seoul says Kyiv requested secrecy about the transfer, fearing domestic criticism for passing up the opportunity to exchange them for “a large number” of Ukrainian prisoners. South Korea says it agreed, citing the safety of the two men and their families as well as diplomatic and security considerations. After Zelenskyy revealed the transfer in his UN speech, Lee said on X that Ukraine had broken a “non-disclosure agreement” and that this was regrettable. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn responded on Facebook that there had been no such agreement, prompting accusations from Lee’s critics that the president, whose approval rating has hit a low of 37.9%, had lied. Lee’s office called Kyiv’s statement “false” and said its conduct “seriously damages trust” between the two governments. On Monday, the foreign ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires, demanding an apology at governmental level. Was there actually an agreement? South Korea’s foreign ministry told Ukraine’s envoy there had been a “clear agreement”. Asked by the Guardian the same day whether anything had been put in writing, the ministry said only that the two sides “had decided to handle it confidentially”. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not respond to a request for comment. Has North Korea said anything? No. South Korea’s unification ministry said it had “not identified any related developments so far” and would continue monitoring. North Korea has glorified soldiers who killed themselves rather than be captured. The transfer of two who survived and chose the South is “a fatal matter” for Pyongyang, says Cho Han-bum of the Korea Institute for National Unification. Having built a “heroic narrative” around its troops, the regime is unlikely to disclose the transfer domestically, he says. How big a diplomatic incident is this? After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, South Korea condemned Moscow’s actions, joined western sanctions and, in July, pledged a $100m support package. But it has kept the war at arm’s length, refusing to send weapons directly to Kyiv, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Before the war, Russia was one of South Korea’s biggest trading partners. Lee’s government is also keen to improve relations with Pyongyang. The row has turned that cautious support for Kyiv into open criticism, largely from Lee’s own camp. Kim Byung-joo, a Democratic party lawmaker, said there was “no reason or need” to support Ukraine and has urged the government to review its aid “immediately”. Photograph: Deborah Cole/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Stolpersteine for the Reiner family, who lived near Heidenau’s railway station. Photograph: Deborah Cole/The Guardian Germany The German town where the right has banned new ‘stumbling stones’ for Nazi victims Heidenau council has halted the laying of Stolpersteine installed to remember individual victims of the Nazis Deborah Cole in Heidenau, Germany Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The town hall of Heidenau, Germany has a freshly restored cream-coloured facade, tidy flower boxes on the windowsills and a charming shingled clocktower. At the entrance, closer inspection reveals a single brass plaque embedded in the pavement honouring the former mayor Paul Gröger, whom the Nazis hounded into killing himself. The plaque is one of 128,000 Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) across Europe, a donor-funded project keeping alive the memory of individual victims of the Nazi era. It is by some measure considered the world’s biggest grassroots memorial project , and has become an integral part of Germany’s “ remembrance culture ” for the atrocities committed under Adolf Hitler. But last week at the same town hall, the council of Heidenau voted to halt the laying of future stumbling stones. In a decision that drew a national outcry , the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party joined forces with the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to help form the majority. View image in fullscreen Anne Nitschke accused the local council of trying to drive the memory of Holocaust victims out of the town centre. Photograph: Anne Nitschke “They want to drive the victims’ memory out of the city centre, just like the victims themselves were driven out,” said Anne Nitschke of AKuBiZ, a citizens’ group coupling history education with pro-democracy work in Saxony state, a hotbed of rightwing extremism . “The point of the Stolpersteine is that you stumble across them every day and then think about who lived here and who was forced to leave,” said Nitschke, 40. Her organisation had filed for permission to lay another 12 plaques for Holocaust victims, until the Heidenau council stopped them. The vote came in a month in which the anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin AfD widened a lead at the top of the national polls, won two state elections and performed strongly in a third, in the capital, Berlin. Like the other mainstream parties, Merz’s CDU has ruled out cooperation with the far right in a stance known as the “ firewall ”. But political realities have often made the AfD an unavoidable partner in municipal policymaking, particularly in the former communist east. Supporters of the stumbling stones ban criticised that their placement on the ground meant they were walked on and exposed to the elements. They called for a “memorial space” in a Christian cemetery north of town “for the victims of war, terrorism, dictators and forced displacement”. Nitschke noted that the council had not made any plans or committed funding for such an endeavour, and said the broad spectrum cited served to deny the “singularity of the Holocaust”. Merz’s national CDU referred queries to the Heidenau chapter, which did not respond to a request for comment. The AfD began as a Eurosceptic party 13 years ago and has morphed into an increasingly nationalist force. It has long targeted memory culture as detrimental to patriotism. One of its founders, Alexander Gauland, compared the Nazi period to a “ speck of bird shit in over 1,000 years of successful German history”. The Saxony-Anhalt chapter, which won a record 44% of the vote in September , pledged to “liberate” Germans from shame over the Holocaust while offering “more Bismarck, less Hitler” in schools. And the part’s co-leader, Alice Weidel, falsely called the Nazi leader “a communist, socialist guy” in a campaign appearance with Elon Musk last year. (The tech billionaire told AfD supporters at the event there was “frankly too much of a focus on past guilt” in Germany.) Many residents of the town said they supported the Stolpersteine and were sceptical of the councillors’ motives. View image in fullscreen Residents such as Christine Bauer, 85, oppose the ban. Photograph: Deborah Cole/The Guardian “Why would they have anything against the Stolpersteine ? It’s easy enough to walk around them if you don’t want to step on them,” said Christine Bauer, 85, who uses a rolling walker to move about town. “I’m a child of the war and remember its awful aftermath,” said Bauer, who worked on Elbe river ships until she retired. “It’s not as if the town council didn’t have bigger problems to worry about now,” she added, mentioning affordability. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion But Silke Schutz, 63, a baker who called herself a “staunch AfD voter”, described the Stolpersteine as “a waste of money, regardless of who pays for them”. “There are so many victims no one cares about,” she said, citing people killed in traffic accidents. “We had nothing to do with the war and at some point it [remembrance] has got to come to an end. But when I express my opinion, I’m insulted as a Nazi.” Started by the artist Gunter Demnig in the 1990s, the Stolpersteine are laid before a Nazi victim’s last home or workplace and inscribed with stark biographical details: date of birth and the date and circumstances of their death. Heidenau has five, all laid personally by Demnig. He reacted angrily to the town council’s decision, calling it a “unprecedented” and wrong. Four plaques are laid just a few minutes’ walk from the Heidenau railway station in honour of the Reiner family. Its Jewish patriarch, Maximilian, ran a local department store until he was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1943. He survived and, after liberation two years later, emigrated to the US and died soon after, in 1949. Gröger, the Social Democratic mayor until 1933, refused to run up the swastika flag at the town hall and was removed from office. In June, Nazi officers spirited him away to the Hohnstein concentration camp, where they beat and tortured him. In August, he took his own life. School pupils raised the funds for his plaque, while AKuBiZ sponsored the remaining four Stolpersteine . Descendants often travel from abroad to attend their installation, as most Holocaust victims lack a gravesite. Local residents support the project by regularly polishing the Stolpersteine , and digital apps provide detailed information about the victims’ fates. Nitschke said no plans had been announced to remove any of the existing Stolpersteine , but for now the 12 planned plaques were on hold, including for Fritz Goldstein , a Jew whom the Nazis stripped of his property and deported to the Soviet Union with his wife, Martha. He died a broken man aged 50, five years after his return to Heidenau. Juliane, 29, a music teacher who declined to give her last name, said she found it moving to learn about the victims through the Stolpersteine . “It is so important we don’t forget, so we don’t make the same mistakes again.” But 28-year-old Philipp, a cook, said he supported the town council’s ban. “It’s not relevant to me – it’s in the past. So there’s no point in dwelling on it now. At some point, you’ve got to put it behind you.” He said Germany’s memory culture had been imposed from abroad. “Other countries just want Germany to constantly have to justify what it did.” Nitschke said her team planned a legal challenge to the ban. This weekend they will lead a march through town to the sites of the planned new Stolpersteine , recounting the stories of each of the victims.
